📈 Composition, stock status and trends

Source: vignettes/articles/status-trends.Rmd
status-trends.Rmd
📦 Data: FAO Global Capture Production, release 2026.1.0 (published by FAO on 2026-03-30; catches 1950–2024), downloaded from Capture_2026.1.0.zip. Licence CC BY 4.0. fao_data_info() shows the release you use and how to cite it.

The summary analyses take any catch data: a fishing area from fishing_area_data(), or any subset of load_fao_data() (see 💾 FAO data). Their charts are saved in figures/png/summary/ and their tables in tables/, with the name of the area at the start of the file names (or label). Each function also returns its results invisibly, so they can be assigned and used in R.

FAO27 <- fishing_area_data("Atlantic, Northeast")

⚙️ Common arguments

Most functions of this article share these arguments; the tables of each function list only its own arguments.

Argument Meaning Default
area_data FAO catch data: fishing_area_data()$area_data, or any subset of load_fao_data() (e.g. one country, or several fishing areas) required
plot Save the charts in figures/png/summary/ TRUE
table Save the tables in tables/ TRUE
lang Language of the chart text and names: "en", "zh" or "both" NULL: the language of fao_settings() ("en" unless changed)
pptx Also save the charts as editable PowerPoint files in figures/pptx/summary/ FALSE; fao_settings(pptx = TRUE) changes it for all functions
label Name at the start of the output file names NULL: the fishing area of the data (or its country; "selected_data" for several areas and countries)

🧺 Species group composition

species_group_composition() sums the catch by ISSCAAP species group (the FAO classification of species into about 50 groups, such as “Herrings, sardines, anchovies”) or by major group (fishes, crustaceans, molluscs, …). FAO gives no Chinese names for the groups; the Chinese names used are unofficial translations.

groups <- species_group_composition(FAO27$area_data)

The first chart shows the catch of each group, the second its share of the yearly catch. The top_n largest groups are shown separately, the others combined. The table gives the mean yearly catch of each decade, the catch of each of the last five years and the share of each group in the last year (tonnes and %):

🚦 Stock status plots

stock_status() classifies the catch series of each species every year, by its catch relative to the peak catch of the series (Kleisner et al. 2013):

Status Rule
Developing before the peak year, catch at most 50% of the peak
Exploited catch above 50% of the peak
Over-exploited after the peak, catch between 10% and 50% of the peak
Collapsed after the peak, catch below 10% of the peak
Rebuilding after a collapse, catch back between 10% and 50% of the peak 
status <- stock_status(FAO27$area_data)

The first chart is the share of stocks in each status, the second the share of the catch. A “stock” here is one species item in the data (all countries together), and years after the last reported catch count as zero catch. Only series that meet the inclusion criteria are classified:

Argument Meaning Default
taxon_levels Taxonomic levels of the items included: any of "species", "genus", "family" and "higher" (pooled groups such as “Marine fishes nei” are "higher") c("species", "genus", "family")
min_years Minimum number of years from the first to the last year with catch 10
min_consecutive Minimum number of consecutive years with catch 5
min_catch Minimum total catch of a series (tonnes) 1000
smooth Smooth the catch with a 3-year running mean before classifying FALSE
area_data, plot, table, lang, pptx, label See Common arguments

The table of stocks gives the peak year and the status of each stock in the last year:

# Smoothed catches, stricter inclusion
stock_status(FAO27$area_data, smooth = TRUE, min_catch = 10000, label = "FAO27 smoothed")

Output: <label>_stock_status_stocks.png and <label>_stock_status_catch.png, and the tables <label>_stock_status.csv (stocks and catch by status and year) and <label>_stock_status_stocks.csv; the function returns yearly, stocks and status (the status of each stock in each year).

Stock status plots use catch data only. A falling catch can also come from management, markets or reporting, so the results are indicative and do not replace stock assessments.

⛰️ Peak and trend

peak_trend() finds, for the total and for the main species (or countries, or areas), the year and size of the peak catch, the catch in the last year as a percentage of the peak, and the trend over the last recent_years years:

  • growth rate (growth_pct_per_year): the average yearly growth between the first and the last of these years, 100[(Cn/C1)1/(n−1)−1]100\,[(C_n/C_1)^{1/(n-1)} - 1], with C1C_1 and CnC_n the catch of the first and the last of the nn years;
  • trend: a Mann-Kendall test (Mann 1945; Kendall 1975), Kendall’s τ between year and catch. Catch series are autocorrelated, which makes the usual test find too many trends, so its variance is corrected with the effective sample size of an AR(1) process (Yue and Wang 2004), from the lag-1 autocorrelation of the detrended series corrected for its small-sample bias (Kendall 1954; lag1_autocorrelation). p_value is the corrected p value and p_value_iid that of the usual test. trend is "up" or "down" when p_value < 0.05, otherwise "none". Over ten years the correction is only partial: strongly autocorrelated series still show trends too often.
  • many series: among ten or more series, some show a trend by chance. q_value adjusts the p values for the number of series in the result, the total excepted (Benjamini and Hochberg 1995). Read trends with p_value < 0.05 as exploratory and give as significant those with q_value < 0.05; 📝 the report does this for its main species and countries.
species_trend <- peak_trend(FAO27$area_data, by = "species", top_n = 10)
show_table(species_trend[, c("name", "peak_year", "pct_of_peak", "growth_pct_per_year", "kendall_tau", "p_value", "q_value", "trend")])
name peak_year pct_of_peak growth_pct_per_year kendall_tau p_value q_value trend
p Total 1976 59.53 -2.0050033 -0.33 0.21 NA none
p1 Atlantic herring 1965 33.48 -0.4745389 -0.20 0.71 0.95 none
p2 Atlantic cod 1969 35.50 -5.2914437 -0.82 0.03 0.16 down
p3 Capelin 1977 4.47 -13.1229391 -0.02 1.00 1.00 none
p4 Blue whiting(=Poutassou) 2004 75.75 2.9400918 0.16 0.74 0.95 none
p5 Atlantic mackerel 2014 65.39 -3.1263873 -0.38 0.33 0.83 none
p6 Sandeels(=Sandlances) nei 1997 7.78 -12.5836285 -0.47 0.07 0.25 none
p7 European sprat 1975 34.92 -5.7343149 -0.82 0.00 0.01 down
p8 Saithe(=Pollock) 1974 41.41 0.4885031 0.11 0.84 0.95 none

area_overview() reads the FAO data itself, so it has no area_data or label. Output: marine_areas_catch.png, marine_areas_peak_trend_area.png and the table marine_areas_peak_trend_area.csv; the function returns the data frame of peak_trend().

🔀 Synchronous breakpoints

regime_shift() runs a breakpoint analysis on the catch series of the main species (all species items, including “nei” groups) and counts how many species change their mean catch in each year. Each series is split where its mean changes (strucchange::breakpoints(), Bai and Perron 2003; Zeileis et al. 2002, 2003), with the number of breakpoints chosen by BIC; the year of a breakpoint is the first year of the new period. Years when many species change together may point to an ecosystem-wide regime shift, or to changes in management or reporting.

shifts <- regime_shift(FAO27$area_data, top_n = 20)
show_table(shifts$breakpoints[, c("species", "first_year", "n_breakpoints", "breakpoint_years")], n = 20)
species first_year n_breakpoints breakpoint_years

Argument Meaning Default

area_data, plot, table, lang, pptx, label See Common arguments

🐟 Pelagic/demersal ratio

pelagic_demersal() divides the catch of pelagic fishes by the catch of demersal fishes (P/D) in each FAO marine area, by year and by decade. Caddy (1993) proposed that nutrient enrichment favours short-lived plankton-feeding pelagic fishes over demersal fishes, and de Leiva Moreno et al. (2000) used P/D as a proxy for the nutrient level of the seas around Europe. The ratio of a decade is the mean of its yearly ratios (as Hondorp et al. 2010), with the lowest and the highest.

pd <- pelagic_demersal(FAO27$area_data)
show_table(pd$decades[, c("period", "pd_mean", "pd_min", "pd_max", "counted_pct")])
period pd_mean pd_min pd_max counted_pct

1960s 0.85 0.35 1.18 79.60
1970s 0.34 0.26 0.43 64.27
1980s 0.29 0.24 0.34 66.68
1990s 0.48 0.34 0.59 68.98
2000s 0.56 0.44 0.78 75.38
2010s 0.52 0.43 0.67 72.70
2020s 0.46 0.42 0.54 74.33

"grainger_garcia" (Grainger and Garcia 1996) Small pelagics, tunas and billfishes, miscellaneous pelagic fishes Flounders, cods and hakes, miscellaneous coastal and demersal fishes, sharks and rays, unidentified marine fishes

Your own groups can be given with pelagic = ... and demersal = .... The published studies classed each species rather than ISSCAAP groups, so their values (below 1 in oligotrophic seas, about 1 to 3.5 in mesotrophic and about 6 to 20 in eutrophic seas, in de Leiva Moreno et al. 2000) are only roughly comparable. P/D also changes with fishing and markets (demersal fishes are in higher demand; Caddy et al. 1998), hypoxia (Hondorp et al. 2010), the natural variability of small pelagics and reporting; see ?pelagic_demersal. In area 27, P/D stays below 1 (by decade, between 0.29 and 0.88) although pelagic species are among the main catches: blue whiting, a pelagic gadoid, is counted with the cods, hakes and haddocks, and Atlantic mackerel (miscellaneous pelagic fishes) is not counted by this definition, which shows how much the grouping matters.

Argument Meaning Default
definition Groups counted as pelagic and demersal: "de_leiva_moreno" or "grainger_garcia" "de_leiva_moreno"
pelagic, demersal Your own ISSCAAP groups (English names as in the FAO data, e.g. "Herrings, sardines, anchovies") instead of those of definition NULL
by "area", or "division" for the catch by division of load_fao_divisions() (🧩 extension) "area"
area_data, plot, table, lang, pptx, label See Common arguments

Inland areas are left out with a message. Output: <label>_pelagic_demersal_ratio.png (P/D by year, one panel per area), <label>_pelagic_demersal.png and ..._share.png (pelagic, demersal and other catch), and the tables <label>_pelagic_demersal.csv, ..._decades.csv and ..._groups.csv; the function returns yearly, decades and groups.

🧩 By division (extension)

De Leiva Moreno et al. (2000) compared the divisions of the Mediterranean and Black Sea. The same units are available from the catch data of regional fishery bodies, loaded with load_fao_divisions() (an extension of the package, not part of the Word report; see 🚢 Trade and employment for the other datasets):

pelagic_demersal(load_fao_divisions("GFCM"), by = "division")

In release 2026.1.0, the mean P/D of the 1980s is below 1 in the Ionian (0.6) and the Levant (0.4), about 4 in the Adriatic and about 18 in the Black Sea, within the ranges de Leiva Moreno et al. (2000) found for oligotrophic, mesotrophic and eutrophic seas.

📝 In the Word report

fao_report() writes these analyses into the Word report of a fishing area (see 📝 Assessment report: Word, LaTeX and PDF). The ISSCAAP groups (groups = TRUE) and the stock status plots (status = TRUE) are sections by default; the pelagic/demersal ratio is added with pelagic = TRUE. The settings of a function are given with the section name as prefix, e.g. status_smooth = TRUE is smooth = TRUE of stock_status():

fao_report(27, pelagic = TRUE, status_smooth = TRUE, pelagic_definition = "grainger_garcia")

peak_trend() gives the trends in the tables of the main species and countries of the report; area_overview() and regime_shift() are not part of it.
